blocks.text: Why real estate analysts struggle with Excel on Mac

Most real estate analysts operate in a high pressure environment where speed and accuracy define success. You deal with massive rent rolls, complex property tax assessments, and multi year cash flow projections. When you work on a Mac, the interface can sometimes differ from the Windows version your colleagues use. This causes friction when you search for specific tools or shortcuts.

Data preparation is your biggest bottleneck. You spend hours importing CSV files from property management systems, cleaning up inconsistent date formats, and fixing broken links. If you spend 80 percent of your time cleaning data, you only have 20 percent left for the actual underwriting. This is where Lazur helps. You can hold your shortcut and ask where a specific tool is or how to fix a recurring error.
Essential Excel shortcuts for Mac users

Memorizing these shortcuts keeps your hands on the keyboard. If you forget one, simply ask Lazur to point it out or explain the function. You do not need to pause your work to search through help menus.
How to handle large datasets in Excel

When you manage a rent roll with thousands of units, performance matters. Start by removing unnecessary formatting. Large files often slow down because of excessive borders or conditional formatting rules that apply to entire columns. Try to apply rules only to the specific range you need.
If you are struggling with a complex formula, ask Lazur to explain it. It can break down nested IF statements or XLOOKUP syntax so you can see exactly where the logic fails.

blocks.text: Common mistakes in real estate underwriting

The most common mistake is hardcoding values into formulas. Always use named ranges or specific cell references. This makes your model easier to audit and update. Another frequent error is ignoring the impact of circular references. These often appear in debt service calculations. Check your status bar to see if Excel warns you about these.

Data types also cause issues. Excel often treats phone numbers or property IDs as numeric values, which strips out leading zeros. Always format these columns as text before you import your data. If you already have the data in Excel, use the Text to Columns feature under the Data tab to fix it.

Lazur lives in your Mac notch. Hold Option + Command to ask about anything on your screen. It answers out loud, saving you from switching tabs or searching through documentation. It does not click buttons for you, but it guides you through every step of a complex process.

Real estate analysis requires multiple apps open at once. You might have Excel for the model, a browser for property research, and a PDF viewer for the offering memorandum. Use your Mac spaces to keep these separate. Dedicate one space to Excel and another to your research. This reduces the cognitive load of switching between contexts.

Keep your file naming consistent. Use a standard format like YYYYMMDD_PropertyAddress_Version. This makes it easier to find files later when you need to reference a specific underwriting assumption. If you need to dictate notes into a cell or a document, hold the fn key to use Lazur's dictation. It is clean and handles technical terms well.

Start by auditing your most used spreadsheet. Check for hardcoded values and simplify your formulas. If you find yourself repeating the same task, look for a keyboard shortcut or a way to automate the process with a macro. Lazur can walk you through the steps to record a macro if you are not sure where to start.
